name: Gambler's Fallacy
description: After a run of one outcome, people feel the opposite outcome is 'due' even when each event is objectively independent. The mind mistakes short streaks for evidence that chance should self-correct immediately.
design_relevance_note: Relevant anywhere products surface streaks, probabilities, or pseudo-random rewards: loot boxes, recommendation rotations, experimentation dashboards, sports-betting UX, or any interface where users infer too much from short runs of outcomes.
prevalence_note: Very widely known in general behavioral-science discourse and familiar in gaming/gambling adjacent design discussions, but not as universally invoked in everyday UX reviews as defaults, anchoring, or social proof.

findings.description: In binary prediction tasks built around a virtual roulette wheel, people showed the gambler's fallacy when independent outcomes were experienced sequentially: after streaks, they predicted reversal more than the same evidence justified. Presenting the identical history all at once attenuated the effect, suggesting the time-based experience of streaks is itself a meaningful antecedent of the bias.
findings.source_title: The role of experience in the Gambler's Fallacy

applications.title: A 135-investor survey: the longer a stock trend runs, the more investors bet it will reverse
applications.description: A survey of 135 Chinese stock-market investors found that the longer a stock's price had been rising, the more investors expected it to fall (and were inclined to sell), and the longer a price had been falling, the more they expected a rebound -- a gambler's-fallacy pattern in real trading behavior, moderated by investors' market knowledge, experience, age, and gender (more knowledgeable and older investors showed the effect less; women were more likely to sell after a price rise, men more likely to sell after a price fall).
applications.ethical_note: A real-world illustration of the gambler's fallacy directly costing real investors money through poorly-timed trades, not a designed influence on a user -- relevant to any financial-product interface (trading apps, robo-advisors) that displays price-trend history, since the display itself may cue this exact reasoning error even without any persuasive intent.

applications.title: Asylum judges, loan officers, and MLB umpires all show gambler's-fallacy-driven decision bias
applications.description: A study analyzing real decisions by asylum judges, loan officers, and Major League Baseball umpires (using objective PITCHf/x pitch-tracking data as ground truth for umpire calls) found significant negative autocorrelation consistent with the gambler's fallacy in all three groups: asylum judges were 3.3 percentage points more likely to deny a case immediately after accepting one; loan officers were 23 percentage points more likely to deny a loan after approving the previous one (an estimated 9% of loan decisions affected); and umpires were 0.9 to 2.1 percentage points more likely to call a pitch a ball after one or two consecutive strike calls.
applications.industry_context: immigration law, consumer lending, professional sports officiating
applications.ethical_note: This documents real, quantified, high-stakes consequences of the gambler's fallacy on real people's lives (asylum seekers, loan applicants) and a professional sport, not a persuasion or product-design case. Included because it is one of the most rigorously measured, highest-stakes real-world illustrations of this bias available, using objective ground-truth data (PITCHf/x) rather than self-report.
